utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, may we move quickly into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us bring in the witness as well as counsel assisting the witness. Good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I take this opportunity to introduce Ms. Silvana Asparuhova from Bulgaria who is studying at The Hague University Institute of European studies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mejakic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are waiting for Mr. Zivanovic to enter the courtroom. Very well. Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zivanovic. I don't think you have to introduce yourself again. Mr. Mejakic, before you commence your evidence, although you know very well already, I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "Incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Mejakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies, good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mejakic.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please be mindful of the interpretation. We both need to wait for it to finish. Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D09535 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read it and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page to identify his signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature. I signed the document on 26 November 2013.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether this statement accurately reflects what you said to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom, would your answers be the same as in this statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this statement into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The added part hasn't been redacted, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. We are tendering paragraphs 1 through 51 and we will redact the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. With that understanding, we'll admit it. I take it there would be no objection, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. There is no objection but I make the following observation: That the question and answer statement has a number of leading questions and some legal characterisations, and in my submission the evidential value of the answers are limited by the questions' formulation and goes to the weight of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4138, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and now I'm going to read, in English, a short summary of Mr. Mejakic's statement. After that I will have a couple of questions for the witness. [In English] Mejakic is the former commander of the Omarska Police Station. He is currently serving a sentence in the Banja Luka penal and correctional institution. On March -- on 24 May 1992, there was a clash between the Muslim extremists and the legal forces of the army and police of Republika Srpska which were supposed to establish free passage through Kozarac, Prijedor, and Banja Luka. On that occasion, about 3.500 armed Muslim extremists put up resistance and the fighting lasted three days. A majority of peaceful Muslim citizens, women and children, sought refuge in the town of Prijedor where the political authorities tried to provide them with accommodation. Those authorities were Serbian authorities. All persons were given medical treatment at the Prijedor hospital and the non-Serb population of Kozarac was not prevented from going back to their houses after the attack. Many Muslim extremists who had taken part in the killing of Serbian soldiers and policemen managed to change to civilian clothes and mixed with the civilians. In order to establish the responsibility of the persons who took part in paramilitary organisations, the chief of the Prijedor public security station, SJB, Simo Drljaca, ordered to set up a temporary collection centre on the premises of the Omarska iron mine. The situation was very chaotic. In one period in Prijedor municipality. The corridor to Serbia was closed, the telephone lines in Republika Srpska were cut off. There was no electricity or water and medicines were in short supply and this inevitably affected the civilian population of all ethnic backgrounds as well as the persons brought to the Omarska collection centre. On the ground, Mr. Mejakic never heard or witnessed that anyone from the Serbian leadership planned the ethnic cleansing of the non-Serbian population. All loyal people of Prijedor who accepted the Republika Srpska and its organs of authority could remain in their homes and posts. Nevertheless, a large number of the civilians, not only Muslims and Croats but also Serbs, wanted to leave the area of Prijedor municipality. Non-Serbs who wanted to leave the area because of war, poverty, unemployment, or security reasons were enabled to do so and they could sell, exchange, or leave their property to the municipal authorities, neighbours, or friends. Most of the prisoners of the Omarska collection centre were brought in from the area of Kozarac and the surrounding villages. These persons were captured in case there were reasonable grounds to suspect that they were extremists members of paramilitary units. Among the prisoners, there were also 20 Serbs who had committed certain crimes and posed a threat to the safety of all people. All persons brought in were taken over and assigned to the premises by the persons responsible for the reception. Mr. Mejakic's responsibility was to escort the persons who were to be questioned from the place where they were accommodated to the office of the inspector. The mine administration never fenced off or protected the complex with the other obstacles, and Mr. Mejakic did not have enough police members to seal off the whole mine complex. Mr. Mejakic and his subordinates tried to adhere to the legal regulations and rules of service as much as possible. If there were individual cases of unauthorised treatment of the detained persons, it could have been only individual and not planned and targeted. As a matter of fact, there was a case of a member of security who abused his duty and tried to obtain illegal material and money from the detained person. Disciplinary proceedings were conducted against him and he was expelled from the police. Nobody ever ordered Mr. Mejakic or his subordinates to maltreat, rape, or kill people in the collection centre, and the civilian authorities at the local level never planned or implemented the permanent removal of Bosnian Croats and Muslims from Bosnian Serb-claimed territory of BH concerning Prijedor. The first visit to the Omarska collection centre was made by a delegation from the ARK in mid-July 1992. On that occasion, Stojan Zupljanin, the chief of the Banja Luka Security Service Centre, asked for the immediate dismantlement of the centre. The first visit by journalists was by the ITN from the [Indiscernible], and although they stressed that Mr. Karadzic himself gave them the approval to visit the whole camp, they could only access what Simo Drljaca decided to show them. In August 1992, representatives of the ICRC went to visit the Omarska collection centre and they were enabled to access the whole complex. And that is a short summary. I would like to ask several -- pose several questions to Mr. Mejakic before I hand him over to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, you were the commander of the police station in Omarska. Were you also the commander of the camp in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was Omarska at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: By definition provided by the chief of the public security station Simo Drljaca, it was a collection centre which was temporary in nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why was the centre needed? Was it possible accommodate and interrogate those people at the police station?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: It was not possible to accommodate such a huge number of people in a standard detention unit, and I assume that for that reason it was decided that that complex, that was a former mine, to be reappointed as a temporary accommodation for centre for people who were taken prisoners either during combat or based on intelligence that they had participated in hostilities or that they were members of the enemy forces, extremists, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remind the Chamber how many Serbs and Muslims used to live in Prijedor on the eve of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I know that in total there was 112.000 inhabitants but at the moment I'm not able to give you the proportion with respect to ethnicity. I cannot remember that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If the ratio was close to 50/50, does that mean that over 50.000 Muslims used to live in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber how many of them were detained after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: While the collection and interrogation centre was in existence, about 3.400 people were processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many of them were released and how many of them were sent to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I believe that the ratio is again half/half. I'm not sure. Maybe there were even more of those who were released and were sent to the collection centre in Trnovo [As interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time, were you aware of any irregularities and maltreatment of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, there was no such attitude. It was neither designed or devised or agreed. I repeat, as I said in my statement, but I do not rule out the possibility, and I even know that there were instances of irregularities and crimes committed against the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Transcript, in line 11, it should read "Trnopolje" not "Trnovo." The open collection centre Trnopolje which was not recorded. Would you be so kind to speak slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, who occasioned and caused these irregularities that occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Primarily those were members of paramilitary formations, criminal groups, but there were also instances, albeit very rarely, that it was done by members from the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you or did anyone undertake any measures against these paramilitaries and unauthorised individuals who committed those deeds?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Not at the time. Later on, something was done about it but at the time, as far as I know, no measures were undertaken to establish their responsibility and to bring them to justice. As far as members of the police are concerned, who were involved, I acted in accordance with the order and in accordance with the rules of service, which means that whenever I gathered information about any irregularity, I would inform Chief Drljaca, who was my direct superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were any efforts made to prevent such a practice of unauthorised access and illegal conduct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can only speak about what was done by the security services from the police. However, there were other services involved as well, that is to say units that provided security of the facility, who did not perform their tasks as they should have done. I'm primarily referring to the outer perimeter of security who was supposed to be the first filter of preventing the unauthorised personnel from entering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 1D18424 in e-court? 65 ter 18242. 424. [In English] 18424. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, can you help us to determine who is the sender of this document, who is the recipient, and what the date is?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: This is document of 13 June 1992. It is addressed to the Security Service Centre, to the chief, who at the time was Mr. Zupljanin. It is signed by the public security station Simo Drljaca. I'm familiar with this document. It has been used as the prosecution document as well as the defence document before the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, could you speak more slowly? Please repeat from where you said it has been used as Prosecution document as well as Defence document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll try to speak more slowly. So it was used in my trial both as the defence and the prosecution exhibit. This is a report about the conduct of members of the special detachment of the CSB Banja Luka. This is, in fact, a detachment that was set up in April 1992, and it took part in various combat operations. Concerning their stay in the collection and interrogation centre, I believe that what is stated here is more than sufficient, what is stated here by Chief Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did Mr. Drljaca obtain this information, from whom?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca received this kind of information from me on a daily basis. However, since this concerns the conduct of police officers, which was contrary to the regulations, they were designated and sent to Omarska to help us prevent access by various paramilitary units, gangs, et cetera. However, they turned into something quite opposite. It was actually them who started creating immense problems. First of all for the detainees, and then later for us in the security. I informed Mr. Drljaca on their behaviour on a regular basis. However, most often he ignored that. When he was finally informed about this by Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic and requested him to take certain action, he sent this letter, this report, to the centre chief and the chief of the centre withdrew this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what eventually happened with this special unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the autumn of 1992, this detachment, as well as all the other detachments, were disbanded pursuant to an order of the Minister of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was that at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, that was Mr. Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 18424 is admitted as Exhibit D4139, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in the process in Bosnia how was the issue of the camp commander or a security commander was treated? What was established by the court regarding your role?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I was indicted by this court as the camp commander. The court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in addition to this indictment as the camp commander, it was expanded to include the function of the chief of security. The trial chamber convicted me as the camp commander and the chief of security. However, the appeals chamber, by accepting partially my appeal arguments, determined that I was neither the camp commander nor the chief of security but that I was, rather, at the head of the security service but only the portion that involved the police forces in that compound.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 65 ter 10970?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This contents from the previous document, was that an exception or was the attitude of the entire police Prijedor consistent with this document? Can you tell us more about the document which is on the screen? Who is the person who submitted this official note?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: This official note was compiled and submitted by Dusko Sikirica, commander of Keraterm security, and it's dated 4th of July 1992. It pertains to criminal conduct of specific individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document and at this point I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, these individuals mentioned here, have they been prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, two of them were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Now we will receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4140, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mejakic, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in its most part in writing; that is, through your written statement. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, you've come here to testify about your role in the functioning of the Omarska camp in 1992. You were tried and convicted in 2008 by the Bosnia-Herzegovina state court of crimes committed against non-Serbs in the Omarska camp, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were convicted of crimes against humanity and sentenced to a long-term imprisonment of 21 years?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Specifically that was crimes of murder; imprisonment, which was the arbitrary and unlawful confinement of camp detainees; torture, including beatings and other physical assaults; sexual violence, which was rapes and other forms of sexual abuse; persecution; and other inhumane acts, including confinement of the detainees in inhuman conditions, harassment, humiliation, and other psychological abuse. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the legal qualification contained in article 172 of the criminal code of Bosnia-Herzegovina, crimes against humanity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you gave evidence in your own trial for five days, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that you appealed the verdict but your sentence was upheld, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. My appeal was partially accepted, but as regards the sentence, it wasn't changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 14 of the statement you've signed in the last few days, you said that there was enough drinking water but conditions for personal hygiene couldn't be at the required level in the given situation. In fact, the accommodation of the detainees was well below any level of decency, the rooms were overcrowded, and hygiene was non-existent since the detainees could have no bath and they had no access to toiletries, right? That was something that you said that the court noted that you had said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Concerning drinking water, this issue, if I'm not wrong, was resolved before this Tribunal in the Kvocka case. It was established that the water used by detainees was drinkable. The access to water sources was there. I have no intention of disputing the fact that the conditions were below standard. I'm talking about this as a professional policeman. These conditions were not suitable for keeping people in detention. However, it was war. An order for issued for them to be detained there. So there was nothing else I could have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The toilet facilities were in an extremely poor condition and a terrible stench pervaded throughout the hangar building throughout these facilities and you testified to that, right? That's what you said in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the court noted that you also said that the food was of low quality, that the detainees were only given one meal a day, and that sometimes some detainees would have no meal at all? You recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I recall saying that in the first couple of days, there was no organised preparation and distribution of one single meal. Later on, the system was established, they received one meal a day, but that was insufficient, and I stand by it to this date when I say that there was not enough food.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the Bosnian court found that the conditions of the camp were brutal and degrading, which resulted in an atmosphere of terror with the detainees, and the court found that detainees were kept without basic necessities of life such as adequate food, which we've just discussed; drinking water, they said was inadequate; medicines and medical care; and the detainees were kept in an unhygienic and in cramped conditions. The court also found that the detainees were subjected to interrogations, beatings, torture, harassment, humiliations, and psychological abuse on a daily basis, and they were living -- and the detainees were living in constant fear for their own lives. And the court found that at least 100 detainees were killed or died as a result of those conditions. You're aware of that finding? "Yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of the court findings. I know for what I was sentenced, but as I said, I came here to tell the truth, and I will do, to the best of my knowledge and memory, to tell the truth about everything. I know very well why I was convicted and I know very well what the trial chamber judgement is and what the appeal judgement is in terms of their contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move now to your statement. In paragraph 10, you said that detainees would be taken by guards for questioning by operative inspectors. You make no mention, though, in that paragraph as to what happened to the detainees during interrogation. And it's right that you heard raised voices and derogatory ethnic terms being used in the interrogation rooms. You admitted that, didn't you, during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: When I was explaining how the security service functioned --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, if can get you to pause there. My question was very simple. I said you said when you were giving your evidence that you heard raised voices and derogatory ethnic terms being used in the interrogation rooms. "Yes" or "no"? That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also heard the screaming of detainees being beaten, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified that many detainees were physically assaulted during their interrogations.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said people would leave the interrogation offices covered with blood, both lightly and seriously injured. That's correct, isn't it? You said that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there were also cases where people, after the interrogation, would die soon after. You testified to that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were telling the truth when you said that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In fact, almost every day somebody would be beaten up, one day it would be five or six, another day seven or eight, and then it would happen that nobody would be beaten up, but this was very seldom. You testified about that too, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I put it that way exactly, but it is possible. It has been about five years since I gave evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is on day 4 of your testimony at pages 84 and 85. I will read the full quote for you. "I mean, when a person comes out beaten up from their office and what I heard from the others, I can claim that almost on a daily basis they would be beaten up. Almost every day somebody would be beaten up. Only once in a while there would be a day when nobody was beaten up, but it was very rarely." And then you were asked: "When it did happen, was it the case that many detainees were beaten up during the course of the day's interrogations? On any given day, is it the case that usually was more than -- was more than one just one detainee who was beaten by the interrogators?" And you said: "More than one is 100 or so, but it wasn't 100. It's a relative thing. One day it would be five or six, another day seven or eight, and then it would happen that nobody would be beaten up. But as I said, it was very seldom." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could it be uploaded so that the witness see his own words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And also only in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And maybe in B/C/S, but let's see whether the witness can remember or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, do you recall that passage of testimony that I just read to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember that portion at the moment. Listen: Last time when I met Mr. Karadzic and his advisers in the presence of my Defence counsel, it was the first time that I found out that there was a written transcript of my testimony because it was not the practice in the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least in my trial, to have a transcript. I had never received this transcript. It was only last night that I heard about this -- its existence and I suppose that it has been compiled subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, I would like you to put a pause on yourself -- on your part as well. I think witness answered yes after your first question in line 13 on page 22, but it was not noted in the transcript. And you've just overlapped with your second question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, so far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like the court reporters to take a look into the audio recording where the witness said yes to the first question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can actually ask Mr. Mejakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You have so far for all the propositions that I've put to you, you have answered in the affirmative that that's what you actually said, didn't -- haven't you? Except for this last one that you were saying you can't remember.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Apart from the last one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But getting back to the level of beatings that were occurring, you don't remember saying this. We can call it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's page 65 ter 25703D. Each of the five days of testimony have been broken into A, B, C, D, of that 65 ter exhibit, Your Honour. Page 85. Okay, we see at the top of the page where you said that there were all sorts of injuries both light and serious and there were also cases that people after the interrogation would die soon afterwards. And then towards the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the original in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour, the pages aren't synced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have a B/C/S version, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've been informed it hasn't been uploaded just at the moment. I'm sorry, can we go to the top of that page again, please? This is the -- this is in chief. I'm wanting the cross-examination. It's -- it's tape number 3896. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'll move on. I'll come back to that when I can get the transcript correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, you said in paragraph 17 of your statement that there was a need for additional accomodation, so all free rooms in the mine complex were used including the famous white house. Now, there was a categorisation system in the camp, wasn't there? You explained it briefly in your evidence-in-chief where category 1 were people who were -- the first category of people were those where it was alleged who had no involvement in any activity whatsoever, and then there was another category of people where it was alleged too that they had provided assistance to other persons who may have been involved in armed rebellion, and it was those people that were in this third category. That's right, isn't it, the three categories?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Correct. That categorisation was in terms of the description as you stated was the same but the number was reversed. The first category, as far as I know, although it's better to ask one of those who did the interrogations and classification, as far as I know the first category were extremists. You just need to reverse the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're right. I was simply saying the three different categories that there were, but those that were involved in the armed rebellion were classed as the first category. And individuals in this category were accommodated in the white house, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No, no, not exclusively in the white house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Predominantly?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: It's a very small space, so you couldn't put up there such a number of people. As far as I know, you couldn't put up there the number of people who were in the first category. At the beginning, that notorious white house was not used at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many people do you think were in the white house on a -- on a good day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: It's hard to tell. From 70 to 80, perhaps less.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: But it's difficult after all this time to make an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You in fact said that the white house was crammed full of people. You went there on two or three occasions and that's what you saw, isn't it, that that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you also said that there was no toilet facility in the building?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Correct, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And for the majority of detainees who were detained in the white house, you could see visible traces of injuries, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: The majority? Some of them, yes, but I'm not sure I said the majority. Indisputably there were people, even before, who had been brought there and kept there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that they appeared to be more beaten up than the detainees accommodated elsewhere in the camp, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: That's correct, that's true. But again, I repeat: I'm talking about the category of people who were classified by inspectors as group 1, and it was according to their orders that they were placed in the white house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there were also other prominent people in the white house, including some politicians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I knew only a very small number of these people. I had worked before in Omarska, 25 kilometres from Prijedor, and I knew very few of these prominent people, politicians and others. I learned some things only much later, after all that happened, and some things I learned only in 2003 from the material you showed me, both inculpatory and exculpatory. I learned some details only then such as the names of those people and the posts they had held. I couldn't know it then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Chief of police, Simo Drljaca, he was at the camp every day -- every other day or approximately every other day, wasn't he, that's what you said when you testified?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Correct, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that he stopped by the room where you were?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very seldom, he didn't really stop by. He usually went to the room where two or three people sat who coordinated the entire service of inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's Mirko Jesic, Ranko Mijic and Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You reported to Drljaca though every day either orally and in writing and sometimes both, about events that were going on in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Not every other day. Every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I seem to have heard every other day in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mirko Jesic and Ranko Mijic were also reporting to Drljaca on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, because I know that in the mornings, before leaving and in the afternoon, after returning from Omarska, they had meetings with Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned these layers of security earlier today. You had the VRS on the most extreme ring of the camp. You've also got the TO manning a number of guard posts. And you've got active and reserve police manning the guard posts on the innermost circle near the -- near the camp compound, that's right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The outer ring.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. And you also have the TO manning, for example, in front of and behind the white house?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were members of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there were three shifts of active and reserve police, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you also had the 12 -- how many -- how many people were in each of those shifts?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, from 22 to 25 policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then you had another 12 policemen working directly to the inspectors who would go and get the detainees from wherever they were staying and take them for interrogation, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a group of 12 members, mainly of the reserve police, who, on the orders of Simo Drljaca, had been assigned to inspectors to serve them which means on the inspectors' orders they would go to a certain room, find the person who needs to be brought for interrogation, and then take that person back wherever the inspector says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And all these people that were involved in security, securing the camp, they were all armed with automatic or long-barrel weapons, weren't they, or pistols?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Most of them had automatic rifles, a small number had semi-automatic rifles, and there were some members of the Territorial Defence who had old M48 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there were two light machine-guns located on the roof of the administration building, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Not two. There was one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You spoke earlier today about these groups coming into the Omarska camp to commit crimes. And you spoke about that in paragraph 15 of your statement, unauthorised persons came to the camp. You testified that groups and individuals who came also killed and were beating detainees. That was what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that Zoran Zigic was the most frequent visitor, for want of a better word, who came to the camp. You testified to that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that Zigic and his group would more frequently visit the white house than other parts of the camp, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And men who came with Zoran Zigic included Dusan, otherwise known as Duca Knezevic, you said that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Dusko Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Dusko Knezevic, yes, but what I said then was that I don't want to go into the identity of that person, the question of his identity, because we are talking about Dusko Knezevic who had been tried before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the same case as myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And he was sentenced to 31 years imprisonment, right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For crimes he committed in the Omarska camp and Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Zigic's group also included Dragomir Saponja, Nikola Janjic, and Zeljko Timarac, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, we saw an exhibit a moment ago, I think it's D4140, where it was about Zigic and Timarac and there was one other, you said that two of them had been prosecuted. But that wasn't by the Serbian authorities during the war or even after the war, was it? Dusko Knezevic was indicted here and his case was transferred along with yours to Bosnia in 2006, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't make a mistake when I said they were prosecuted in the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. In the end. Who was the other person -- and Zigic, again, he was the other person of the three that you were referring to, and he was in fact convicted and sentenced by a court at the ICTY to 25 years' imprisonment, wasn't he, for crimes that he committed in Keraterm and Omarska camps? For the record you have to speak louder, I think, so that your answer is on the transcript. You said yes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your trial chamber found that this group of visitors was a synonym for the beating of detainees, especially in the white house. These people weren't stopped by either the VRS, the TO, or the police. And there was no willingness on your part or the Serb authorities in Prijedor to stop these people from entering the camp, was there? To stop them from entering and committing murder and brutal beatings of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: The question is too broad but I'll try to answer. It's not that there was no will, no obligation, to stop these people from doing that. And I don't mean only these groups. I mean some other groups as well. It's quite simply that it was a temporary facility without a fence around it, without any physical barrier between those visitors, quote/unquote, as we call them, and the detainees. There was no physical obstacle. When they pass through the first ring of security, they are already inside, and I did not have either enough personnel or enough resources or any way to stop them. They were well-armed groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If -- if the authorities had wanted to stop this group from -- and other groups from coming into the camp, they had the whole of the 1KK Corps, the 1st Krajina Corps, sorry, the RS MUP. What's to stop them getting reinforcements to stop these people from coming into the camp? They came in because everyone was happy for them to do it.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody, starting with me, and the majority of the policemen and inspectors there, nobody was happy that they were coming in and doing what they were doing. God forbid. A normal person could not be happy about that, about watching people maltreating other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I'm right, because I'm not sure about double negatives in English and in Serbian, but on page 31, lines 10 and 11, the witness said it's not that there was no will or obligation. I don't know how that is understood in English. Maybe we should clear up with the witness. Was there a will and obligation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, there was a will and obligation to stop it, and we did all we could do to stop such occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But you did nothing. They were never stopped from coming into the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Some evidence that was led in court say the opposite. There were examples of witnesses who testified that some people had been stopped in the attempt to mistreat them, extort money, et cetera. There were prosecution witnesses who --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm talking about Zigic's group. Nothing was done to stop them from coming into the camp, and you said that they came into the camp through June and July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I said they were coming throughout June. I don't know about July. But if, with all his authority, Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic who had means to organise people to stop them, how could I be expected to stop them?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were in charge of security. It was your job to protect the detainees. Mr. Mejakic, I'll just read what you said in -- when you were asked to clarify whether you said June or July, you said -- the question was from Defence counsel: "When asked by the Prosecutor you mentioned, if I am not mistaken, with regard to Zoran Zigic, the prosecutor asked you if he would come both in June and July, and you confirmed that he would come to the Omarska camp in both these months; is that correct?" And you said: "I was sure about June and I said I think he also came in July. This is how I said it." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm sure he came in June, and I don't rule out the possibility that he was coming also in July. That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said in paragraph 16 of your statement that two people tried to escape from the camp and were killed. Now, that's the only mention of killings in your statement. You omitted to mention the number of individuals that you know were killed in the camp either because you were in the camp at the time or you were told by Kvocka or Prcac about them being killed, and you actually gave examples and you named around 15 individuals and the circumstances surrounding their death when you testified in Bosnia, but you didn't think it was relevant to include -- to include that you were aware of a number of deaths in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: When I gave that statement, I was answering questions, specifically about two cases when firearms were used by members of the security. There were only three cases when firearms were used by the police security service. I talked about those two cases where two persons were killed, and I spoke about one case where one person was injured, wounded, transferred to the Prijedor hospital, and survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, you're a policeman, and you have been up until 1992, you were a policeman for at least nine years, and you continued on after as a policeman until at least 1996. When you were being -- when you were giving this statement to the Defence and you mentioned that two people had -- you were asked about the two people that had been killed, didn't you think to mention, well, there was a lot of other people killed and let me tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's not in your statement. The only thing that's in your statement is about the two people, the two escapees.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know why it's not in the statement. I said that I can speak in a qualified way only about the police aspect of the work, about the police security service. About the other services down there, I can speak from my own personal knowledge and perhaps hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said at least four individuals died from natural causes, yes? When you testified.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that one of them, Safet Ramadanovic -- Ramadanovic, died a natural death; however, your trial chamber found that he died as a result of injuries sustained during the beating he received from guards Predojevic and Popovic; that's right, isn't it, that's how he died, not of natural causes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. First of all, his name was not Rafah Ramadanovic but Safet Ramadanovic, who died of natural causes. His body was handed over to his family. His mortal remains were handed over to the family who buried the body.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, I'm not disputing whether they were handed over. I'm disputing how he was -- how he died.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I repeat: I am telling you only what I know about the case. This is what my immediate knowledge is. I repeat: I know why I was convicted. I know what it says in my court decision. But I'm here to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you know -- if you know what it says in your court decision, then you'll know that the court found that he was killed by being beaten to death by two guards. That's correct, isn't it? That's the court finding.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: This is what the court established.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: And it would never even occur to me to discuss the contents of the court's finding or to comment upon it. I am a law professional. The court found one thing. I tried to prove that it was differently. Well, what can I say?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, I want to just quickly take you back to the issue we were dealing with when we had the problem with the transcript page coming up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 25703D. Now, Your Honour, there was glitch in that it was the right exhibit number but the wrong document was attached to the number in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And on page 85, you see your answer there, Mr. Mejakic, starting --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- halfway through that paragraph, I can claim that almost on a daily basis, they would be beaten up. Almost every day somebody would be beaten. Only once in a while there would be a day when nobody was beaten up, but it was very rarely. Now, you said that there, didn't you, when you testified in -- in your trial?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is what witness confirmed earlier on. What witness said he couldn't remember is the five or six, or six, seven, so you're not going to show that page?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we could go further over -- further down, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The last --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, the last notation on this page with ZM --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read the question as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The question was: "And when did it happen? Was it the case that many detainees were beaten up during the course of the day's interrogations? On any given day, is it the case that usually it was more than just one detainee who was beaten by the interrogators?" And you replied: "More than one is 100 or so, but it wasn't 100. It's a relative thing. One day it would be five or six, another day seven or eight. And then it would happen that nobody would be beaten up, but as I said it was very seldom." Now, you said that when you testified?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't need that exhibit any more, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, on an almost daily basis, several dead bodies would be seen by witnesses in the camp which would be loaded on to a yellow TAM or Tamic truck and taken away, and that's what your trial chamber found, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: It is correct that the Trial Chamber found that but I repeat: This does not tally with the truth. That's not how the situation was in reality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, numerous witnesses have testified that dead bodies were seen piled up outside the white house on a daily basis. Are you disputing -- are you disputing that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I disputed that during my trial. You are referring to the witnesses who confirmed that. I, however, referred to the equally numerous witnesses who denied that. The trial chamber found what they did, and I don't have the right to proffer any comments on their final judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, you saw a number of dead bodies in the camp including three the morning you first arrived in the camp, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is the truth. As I've told you, I'm here to tell the truth to the best of my knowledge and recollection. However, if we are talking about those three bodies, then we have to be very open and we have to tell the whole truth. Those bodies --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I spoke about that, I said that the -- I found those three bodies when I first arrived at the collection centre or camp, call it what you will. However, none of the security guards from the police ranks was present there during the night when the camp was being established. Those dead bodies were a consequence of what was going on during that first night. As far as I know, nobody dealt with the issue of establishing the responsibility of the perpetrators. Nobody bothered to find out whether those people had tried to escape during transport, how they were killed, who they were, nobody dealt with that. On that same day when I saw those bodies, within the next 45 minutes I informed Chief Drljaca of what I'd seen and what had happened to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay, what about on the one occasion, the only one occasion that you saw a TAM truck stop outside the white house where two bodies were loaded and transported off? You said that in your trial. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise and tell me in what part of my testimony or what dead bodies you are talking about? If at all possible. Because I really did not see the transcript from my trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It was in cross-examination. It was on the -- on the last day of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could bring up, please, 65 ter 257101E, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were asked about the TAM trucks coming to the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter number again?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were asked on page 7, and did you ever see them taking bodies out of the camp --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it released?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 25703E. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Please, if it is possible to have the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She said unfortunately it was not uploaded or it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we see there on page 7, halfway down the page: "And did you ever see them taking bodies out of the camp?" And you said: "The TAM truck that drives a dead body, actually not one but two dead bodies on one occasion." And then you said -- you mentioned the two dead bodies and you believed it was the same situation. So you remember this evidence that you gave? And if we can just go over the page, I'm sorry, to just finish the proposition that I put to you, halfway down the page, the prosecutor says: Did you ever see them stop at the white house, still talking about the TAM truck. Apart from this case where they took two bodies, I didn't see them stopping. Now, you said that in your testimony, didn't you? You can see it there.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: This is the English version. Honestly I don't read English. I would love to see it in a language I understand. I'm not clear on some things here. It is true that in my testimony when I testified before the court, I confirmed the fact that the dead bodies were taken from Omarska in a TAM lorry. I saw that with my own two eyes. I also stated that either two or three dead bodies, including the dead body of Becir Medunjanin, were taken away by the vehicles of the utility company; i.e., they were taken away in a funeral truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You actually limited it to only Becir Medunjanin's body. You said, and this is in your evidence-in-chief, other transport was used to take dead bodies out of the camp. Becir Medunjanin's body was taken away by a vehicle owned by the Prijedor utilities company. You remember saying that, yes? And because of that you surmised that his murder must have been reported to the authorities. You said that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said that. As far as his murder is concerned, like in any other incident, my superior Simo Drljaca was informed. Pursuant to the decision on the setting up of the camp, I was duty-bound to report to him on all the issues concerning security.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you also said, when the Prosecutor was questioning you about the number of persons or bodies that you saw in Omarska, and he had actually counted up in -- as you gave your evidence-in-chief, he came to a figure of around 12 killings. I mentioned 15 this morning. That was -- that was my count on the evidence that you had given in chief. And he was asking you about, you know, he said now the number of bodies that you saw in Omarska, and you gave evidence about the circumstances of each of the killings, and he said to you, how many people, how many detainees, were killed in Omarska? Is that list exhaustive? And you said, to your response, to your question, I cannot give specific answer about the exact number. What -- what's the -- what's the issue on -- on not being able to give an exact number of the number of people that were killed? Was it that there were so many killed that that's why you can't specify a number?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No. No. It's not about that. It's about a very sensitive issue in my humble view, an issue that had not been dealt with in any of the proceedings conducted either before this Court or the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Many speculations exist there. The first figure that was mentioned was 3.800 who were killed, and then 1.000 or 900 or 700. These are terrible things because these are lies that still persist to this very day. It was made impossible to my defence team to cross-examine the prosecution expert who drafted all those reports about all the deaths that occurred in Prijedor municipality. If I'm not mistaken, his name is Nikola Sebauer [phon]. His report was admitted from bar table and he was not cross-examined. I believe that the cross-examination of that witness in my case would have resulted in an approximate number of those who were killed in Omarska. There is yet another thing that needs to be emphasised. Many individuals were last seen alive in Omarska. They left Omarska. And -- and their whereabouts are known from then. However, it is still believed that they were killed in Omarska. You have to take into account the fact that there were cases when the list which was signed by the chief was used by the guards to call up the names of the individuals and the explanation was that they were to be exchanged. I arrived here in 1993 and I learned that those individuals were found dead in Lisac [indiscernible] bit 100 kilometres away from Omarska. That's why I'm saying that I'm not sure about any of that. I spoke about those things that I know, that I saw and experienced myself. I don't want to speculate because the issue is really very sensitive.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, I take it you arrived here in 2003?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 2003, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 41, line 17, the witness said that the issue was not dealt with so far but, rather, that no correct answer was ever provided as to the number of deaths. Yes, people were dealing with that issue but the number was never established. This is what the witness stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm, Mr. Mejakic, having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, the night you saw the three dead bodies in the camp, you had additional information that more were dead, correct? And I simply want a yes or a no to the answer to my question, "yes" or "no," you had additional information that more were dead?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Let me correct you. It was not during that night but in the morning. In the morning when I saw those dead bodies. I did receive some additional information about people who had been killed but not in Omarska but further afield.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said it is possible that seven who were taken away, some seven or eight or 15 kilometres away from the Omarska camp, you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I have just stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, the Tomasica mine is 15 kilometres away from the Omarska camp. Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No, no, I did not refer to that. I meant the areas of Kozarac and Kamicani.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So where were these dead bodies taken, some 7, or 8, or 15 kilometres away, I mean in the places that you've just said? Where specifically were they taken?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that the bodies were taken somewhere. I'm saying that people had been taken away, and as far as I heard, they were killed in that place. I don't know where the bodies were subsequently buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, you spoke about four people being taken to Kozarac and being killed. What location are you referring to when you are referring to 15 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What four people do you have in mind? What four people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The day after the 30th of May, when you -- when you saw the three dead bodies in the camp, you -- you gave evidence that an additional four people were taken and they were taken out of the camp to Kozarac and killed. You gave that evidence. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Are you implying that I said that in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I ever put it that way. I said, and I repeat, that I learned from other people that during that night in addition to the three dead bodies that I subsequently found there, that some other individuals had been taken away from the camp in the direction of Kozarac or Kamicani where they were killed. This is what I said and this is what I am repeating here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So of the -- of the dead bodies that were in the camp, where were they taken? Now you mentioned, for example, that you saw the TAM truck stop by the white house, pick up two dead bodies, and go out of the camp. Where were those two bodies taken?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You didn't -- you didn't ask any questions about where they were being taken?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Why was it worthwhile to ask anyone, since no one could provide an answer? We in the police were told to stick to what our job was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please move closer to the mike and could all the mikes not in use please be switched off while the witness is speaking? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 of your statement, you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, could you come closer to the microphone, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 of your statement, you state that they fabricated a massacre of 250 detainees who were brought from the Brdo area. When you say "they," I presume you're meaning the non-Serb witnesses, no?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to my statement given to Mr. Karadzic's investigators?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, here. If it is no problem, can I be shown?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I could probably give a hard copy with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Or we can upload it as well. Show it to the Prosecutor first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So -- and I don't want to go into the details, Mr. Mejakic, simply I want to know who the "they" are that you're referring to. You're talking about non-Serb witnesses who testified about that particular massacre of people brought from the Brdo? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Can I have a moment to read it, please? As far as I can see, it reads the following: A massacre of about 250 detainees was fabricated, the detainees brought from Brdo which was also not corroborated by evidence. There is a series of other things attributed to Omarska camp. I don't see any personal pronoun here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. It must be the translation. Your trial chamber found beyond any reasonable doubt that the event took place and determined that at least 50 detained inhabitants of the village of Hambarine were killed at the critical time. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Allow me to answer this question. I will to have give you an extensive answer, but I won't take too much of your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Mr. Mejakic. The question is your trial chamber found beyond reasonable doubt that at least 50 detained inhabitants of the village of Hambarine were killed. That's a finding of the trial chamber, isn't it? "Yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was established by the trial chamber, but, please, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. The allegation -- sorry, the allegation was between 100 and 150 people were killed. Your trial chamber found at least 50 were killed. So you're not saying it didn't happen, you're just quibbling about the numbers; is that right? Is that right, Mr. Mejakic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: There was a dispute during the trial whether that happened at all or not. It was also disputable that in the judgement findings about the 50 persons, there was not a single information providing details of these individuals. As far as I know, every individual has a first name and a last name. You won't find that either in the indictment, in the annex to the indictment, or any other documents. You won't find their full names. This is what took place during the trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're aware of a group of around 15 people who were liquidated by a police guard on one of the inspector's say-so, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I believe that this relates to the testimony of Mr. Jesic in the Kvocka trial when he spoke about the execution of 15 or 18 individuals. But this is not about --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, actually, it's your evidence. It's your evidence that you gave at the state court.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But during my testimony, I invoked Mr. Jesic's testimony, and I explained what that was actually about; that is to say, that those people were not killed in Omarska and not by the guards, the police guards. These individuals had been taken away from the Omarska camp and thereon they disappeared without a trace.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your evidence, and this is in your evidence-in-chief, on the third day -- second day, you said: [As read] "On the following day I talked to Jesic Mirko who told me that there is a possibility that the previous day around 15 people were taken away from the camp, and then he started naming the people -- the persons. "And since they requested lists for interrogation, I remember he mentioned Avo Sadikovic, and he was the person I knew. He used to be a crime department inspector. Generally, around 15 days... around," sorry, "15 people were taken away." Now, you remember saying that in your evidence? And then --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I recall now, since you mentioned Inspector Sadikovic's name, I remember talking about this in the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I remember what I said and I stay by it. Of course, on condition that what I said is accurately interpreted in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you said that: [As read] "Mirko Jesic never told me the name of that particular inspector. And I know that since I was trying to find out he told me don't talk about this too much, it can give you a headache, cause a headache to you. This is our job. We'll check it up with Simo. Somebody should be held responsible sooner or later." You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, when Mirko Jesic testified in the Kvocka case he actually said, and this is at transcript page 11753 to 11754, he said: [As read] "Soon after his arrival in the first half of July, when he came to the investigation centre, soon after his arrival he heard that the night before there had been a grave incident and immediately went to see our leader or commander, Zeljko Mejakic. I asked him what happened last night, and he said that several Muslims or rather detainees had been killed in Omarska camp." Then further on: [As read] "After that he told me that it had been done upon a request -- upon the request of an inspector, and Mr. Jesic inferred it must have been Rade Knezevic." Is that right? Was that the inspector that -- that, on -- upon whose orders these 15 or 18, 15 to 18 people were liquidated?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I think that Mirko Jesic, during his testimony, mixed up two incidents. The incident where Inspector Sadikovic is mentioned, that incident took place during day-time, whereas another incident, when people were taken from Omarska, 18 of them, under the pretext that they were being taken to the prison, I think that is where he got it mixed up. There was a confusion in his perception.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So now we've got two groups of 15 being taken away?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have a group of 15 to 18 individuals who were taken away towards Gradiska or to the Gradiska prison, whereas the other incident which took place during day-time involved the taking away of 15 individuals from the collection and interrogation centre and that is the incident that Mirko Jesic and I discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mirko Jesic said that he asked you what Rade had done and he said that -- and you said that he'd given a guard a list of names which in his judgement and according to his demand valuables should be taken and after that they should be liquidated. So who was this guard that got this list of the people by the inspector?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know who this guard was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He's one of your guards. He's one of your guards. You were the one that told Mirko Jesic about the incident when Mirko Jesic turned up for work the next day and you said that this inspector had given one of your guards a list of the people who needed to be liquidated, so I'm asking you who was the name of the guard?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
