utterances.text: No. It's not true that Mirko Jesic and I discussed the name of the guard at all. Even more, Mirko Jesic never said that he was talking about a specific inspector.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You may not have discussed the name of the guard with Mirko Jesic, but in you telling Mirko Jesic about it, you must know who the name of the guard is. Who was the guard that took the names of the 15 people to be liquidated?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Apart from the large number of people that you saw or heard having been killed in the camp, there were also a large number of people that were taken away from the camp and never seen again, and you've just alluded to this -- or two groups, actually, being taken away. So you say that a group in your -- in your evidence in the -- in your own trial, you say a group of about 20 people including, nine or ten people with the surname Garibovic and also Slavko Ecimovic, you say --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: It's Garibovic, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's what I thought I said, Mr. Mejakic. You say these people were taken away around the 20th of June, according to you, for exchange. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember talking about that. I received in translation the name Garibovic whereas the name is Garibovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Those people were killed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I cannot talk about that because I am not aware of that. I assume that they were killed, but the point is that when they left Omarska they were alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, your Trial Chamber found that Slavko Ecimovic was beaten to death by Dusko Knezovic and Zigic around the 10th of June in the camp. You're aware of that finding of the Trial Chamber? "Yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember entirely, but I do remember that in the course of the trial it was proven that Slavko Ecimovic was beaten up in the barracks prior to him being brought to Omarska. And Slavko Ecimovic, to my knowledge, was taken with the group where the majority of people had the last name of Garibovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We have evidence in this case that a number of individuals named Garibovic who were last seen in the Omarska camp in June were exhumed from three mass graves, and that's at Jakarina [phon] Kosa, Stari Kevljani [phon], and Kevljani [phon], and that's at P4855. So there's no dispute that they were killed, is there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: There is obviously nothing disputable there. The only issue at dispute is that whether they were in Omarska or outside Omarska, and what I'm saying is that they were alive when they left Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You are saying nobody left the camp either in groups or individually without a list, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said even if it meant that there was only four people or one person on the list?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that detainees started to be taken away in small and large groups but that it intensified in the last five or six days of July, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say in the last 10 days of the month, of the month of July to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said sometimes there would be three or four transports of people that one or two buses would come two or three times a day to take people away, and that this started from mid-July. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those were the people who were mainly driven to Trnopolje, if they were taken by buses and put up in an open admissions centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, in fact, you were present in the camp when a group of around 45 men and two women were taken out of the camp, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Forty four men and two women.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Drljaca's driver brought the list to the camp and then the men and the two women were called out and put on the bus which then left the camp. You said that when you testified, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you also said that all these detainees were exhumed from a mass grave in Jama Lisac in the Bosanska Krupa municipality. That's what you said when you testified, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said, and I repeated it a minute ago that Grjvlisac [as interpreted] near Bosanska Krupa 100 kilometres, at least 100 kilometres from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the two women that were taken were Edna Dautovic and Sadeta Medunjanin; that's right? Sadeta Medunjanin was a teacher and the wife of Becir Medunjanin who was killed by Zigic and Knezevic and the rest of his group in the white house.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Safeta Medunjanin and Edna Dautovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now these people were officially being taken out of the camp, weren't they? You've just said that nobody left the camp without lists, without a list being provided?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were also present in the camp in the afternoon of the 5th of August when two busloads of detainees were brought from the Keraterm camp weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And were you told that they wouldn't stay there for long, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: The escort who drove them there told me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And later that night, after you'd left the camp, but you were told the following day what had occurred: Drljaca's driver brought a list which said that Dr. Esad Sadikovic, otherwise known as Eso, had to join the Keraterm detainees on the bus, and that Prcac called him out and he boarded the bus and it left. That's what Prcac told you the following day, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that is the evidence that I gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the two busloads of men from the Keraterm camp and Dr. Sadikovic from the Omarska camp didn't survive, did they?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You know because you said it in your testimony they were exhumed from a mass grave in Hrastova Glavica and that some of the bodies recovered were identified? That's what you said, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I explained that that was the knowledge that I acquired long after the war, that is to say that these people had been executed at Hrastova Glavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Which is located in the Sanski Most municipality, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to a document entitled: "Omarska SC, First Category Persons."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could bring up 65 ter -- sorry, Exhibit P5519, please. Mr. Mejakic, we spoke earlier today about the categorisation and you said that the first category were the -- were the people that were alleged to have participated in armed rebellion. Now, this document is dated 28 July 1992, so around a week before the majority of people in the Omarska detention facility is shipped off to Manjaca and Trnopolje, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, these -- if we do a comparison between the names on this list and the names on Exhibit P4855, which is an exhumation document, it's clear that 29 of the -- these people on the list have been exhumed and 27 of which were all exhumed from the mass grave in Jama Lisac in the Bosanska Krupa municipality. So when were these 27 people taken out of the camp and buried -- and taken to Jama Lisac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: The people who were taken away and subsequently exhumed in Jama Lisac were 44 men and 2 women, not 27, 44 men and 2 women. If I'm not wrong, that took place in June, not July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, there is a lot of people that are buried in that mass grave in Jama Lisac, two different things, yes, the 44 and the 2 women were exhumed there, but 27 of 29 people on this list were also exhumed from Jama Lisac. Now, do you know anything about these 27 from the category 1 list?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No. I really don't know anything about this. This is the first time I hear this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, this list has 174 persons. I don't follow, 27 of 29 in your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I misspoke. There are two other names which are very, very close to with -- in relation to father's name and location which could put the number at 29, but at a minimum, there is 27 of these 174, although I thought there was 176. So that's where the figure of 29 comes because there is two other names that are -- have a misspelling in one of either the first name or some other detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We also know that there was two other people on this list, one of who was exhumed in a mass grave -- in a grave outside Banja Luka, and that's because he was transferred and killed on his arrival at the Omarska camp on 6 August 1992. Now, this Trial Chamber has received evidence on the reported dead and missing who were last seen in Omarska camp, and you referred to that earlier on today when you gave an extraordinarily long answer to a question about how many dead bodies had you seen in the camp. The evidence that the Trial Chamber has is Exhibit P4855, and included in that exhibit are the names of people where they have been reported as last seen in places other than Omarska Logor, for example, Kozarac. But where we have evidence, there's evidence been admitted in this case where they were last seen in Omarska Logor. And I'll just read out these figures for you and then I'll ask you a question. So the number of people that were last seen in Omarska Logia and exhumed are 211 people. The number of people last seen in Omarska Logia where no remains have been found is one person. And in addition to that detail about the exhumations, there is also additional victims who were named in our scheduled incidents, and you know from your own case here that the Prosecution appends to their indictment the scheduled incidents that occur, and so in relation to the victims that are named in schedules B15.2, which is the Omarska camp, and B15.3, which is the killing of a number of men and women taken from the Omarska camp in the area called Hrastova Glavica which we discussed a moment ago, so the number of people from that that have been exhumed are 86 that were last seen in the camp, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's stop here. I'm not sure whether the witness is following your question. Could you make your question a bit simpler?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was trying to do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There is four categories of people Mr. Mejakic; the ones that were last seen in Omarska Logia and exhumed, 211; last seen in Omarska Logia where no remains have been found yet, 1; and then the other category are where they're named in our schedules who have reported as being last seen in places other than Omarska Logia, but we have information that puts them as last seen in the camp. That category of people. So, for example, their family member may say, Right I last saw him in Kozarac when he was taken away -- when he was arrested and taken away. But we have information where somebody in the camp, for example, has seen that person after the family member has seen that person, and so then that category of people, there has been 86 people that have been exhumed, last seen in Omarska. And the fourth category was where you have these named people who were reported seen in places other than Omarska, but we have evidence to show that they were -- they were -- they were reported by the family as being found elsewhere, but we have evidence that they were last seen in Omarska, and that category of people is 40 people. So the bottom line is, the evidence in this case is 211 and 86 and 40 and 1, all last seen in Omarska, either dead or missing. 297 exhumed and 41 missing. So that doesn't square very well, Mr. Mejakic, does it, with you saying that nobody was killed in the camp, there were no dead bodies in the camp, does it? This is an extraordinarily high number of people. You've got over 300 people.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that it's a large number of people, but I don't agree with you that I had denied the murders in that room. Never, before the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina or here, have I ever denied that there were killings in Omarska, and you said a moment ago that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The only thing in your statement about killings is in relation to two escapees. That's the only mention of any killings whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I was talking about two murders, two incidents, with which members of the police security service are associated. I was not talking about the killings committed by the so-called visitors. I wasn't talking about the murders or how else could you qualify it if during interrogations somebody is beaten up so badly that they die ten minutes later. I wasn't talking about these things. I was talking about two incidents in which members of the security service were directly involved. In one of these incidents, in the Kvocka trial, a man testified who was involved in that incident as a member of the security detail. During an attempt to escape, he used his gun, and killed the person who had tried to escape. That also happened in the other incident when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So now that I've put all these figures to you, you don't -- you don't deny -- or you will agree, won't you, that there were an extremely large number of people that were killed in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that. If we are talking, let's say, about these 40 plus 2. They were not killed in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, you just -- you just mentioned that people died having succumbed from their injuries after they were beaten in interrogations. You also mentioned that people were killed by these groups that were coming into the camp, not least of all Knezevic and Zigic. There were also instances where people were killed by the police security. So you're not denying that -- that there were a large number of people killed in the Omarska camp, are you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: It's too many if only one person were killed. I don't know what you mean by "a large number of people."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dozens, dozens.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: How many dozens?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, I've just gone through the figures with you, there is over 300 people. There is over 211 people that have been exhumed last seen in Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I have no intention of refuting the accuracy of these figures, but I do dispute that these 120 people who were brought to Omarska and who were joined by Esad Sadikovic, I do deny that they were liquidated in Omarska. They spent only four or five hours in Omarska except Mr. Sadikovic who had been there for a while. So they were not liquidated at Omarska. The members of the security service and all the other people are not involved in these killings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Those two buses from Keraterm certainly aren't included in these figures because they're different figures. That's for the Keraterm camp. That's something else. I'm talking about Omarska at the moment. But let's move on. You -- I want to turn now to some visits of certain delegations that came to the Omarska camp. You said in paragraph 25 of your statement that the first visit to the camp was by a delegation from the Autonomous Region of Krajina in mid-July 1992 and they were led by Zupljanin, Brdjanin, Vukic, and Radic. And you said the delegation was met by Drljaca and that they had a meeting in the administrative building of the mine, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said in your statement that you heard one of the inspectors who attended the meeting that Zupljanin spoke angrily to Drljaca and allegedly asked that this collection centre be dismantled immediately?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We have evidence in this case that Exhibit P01097 that not five days later, Zupljanin wrote to the RS MUP and told Mico Stanisic that he had a large number of men of no security interest who can be treated as hostages. So it doesn't appear to be the position of a man who is urgently wanting to dismantle the camp, does it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know that Mr. Zupljanin wrote such a letter to Stanisic. I am just saying what I heard from the inspector who attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The only reason you're saying this is to push your view that Drljaca is independent, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: It's not my intention to speak of Drljaca with a lot of speculation. I know who Simo Drljaca was. I know that he is a man -- he was a man who didn't brook any authority, and he did mostly as he pleased.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, not two weeks -- not two weeks later, Zupljanin retroactively appointed Drljaca as the chief of the Prijedor police. So he can't have been too displeased with him, can he? And that's Exhibit P06379. I mean, if he's so displeased with him, why appoint him? Retroactively, I might add.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know about that letter of appointment. I only know that between Drljaca and Zupljanin, there was not much cooperation and they didn't see eye to eye on many things.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, that is not true. The evidence in this case shows that there was continual reporting backwards and forwards between the CSB Banja Luka and the Prijedor SJB. Drljaca was filing quarterly, six-monthly, yearly reports, responding to dispatches.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was an obligation. The public security station is under the purview of the Security Services Centre, so it was their obligation to report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You just said a moment ago that he did mostly as he pleased. He didn't. He was actually toeing the line.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Whether he was toeing the line or not, I don't know. All I know is what his attitude was to the management, to the leadership, of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mention in paragraph 25 of your statement the first visit by the foreign media, and you said that the delegation said that they had approval from Karadzic to accession the whole mine complex that Drljaca responded: "I don't care about that approval. You will visit what I tell you and you can complain to Karadzic." You remember putting that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was there when it was said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to show you the video footage of the visit, and -- and what was actually said to the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could play P03785, please, from 00.39 through to 02.12.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. That's one of the shift commanders, Mladjo Radic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And witness's answer was not recorded to your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, you agreed with me that that was Mladjo Radic in the frame standing in the --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, we see here in front of us -- who is the person on the left of the screen?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: On the left is major or lieutenant colonel of the Army of Republika Srpska, Milutinovic, head of the press centre of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the one on the right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: On the right is Simo Drljaca, chief of the public security station Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can keep playing, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "Interpreter: They say this is an investigation centre, so if they prove that they are guilty or not guilty and there is also the procedure, so this is a centre for investigation. "Penny Marshal: Yes, why can't we see?... "Interpreter: So that's -- you cannot see that. "Penny Marshal: They just said upstairs that anyone could see it, the Red Cross couldn't come and now they're stopping us. We've seen nothing. We've seen one dinning hall and 80 prisoners." "Male Reporter: But we have a promise from Dr. Karadzic and now they're telling us something else. "Interpreter: All of them are going. "Guard: Here they are waiting. "Male Reporter: We cannot, we cannot make a proper judgement about this camp until we see the way they live."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, shall we stop it. Would you like the witness to hear this portion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think there is any translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just while we have this still on the screen, Mr. Mejakic, who is -- who is - that's you in the centre of the frame, isn't it, with the blue beret?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, if we can keep playing the footage is at the -- I will go to another clip in a moment. If we can keep playing --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. For the benefit of the [Microphone not activated] Court I ask the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Court, perhaps the interpreters could interpret this conversation if we can rewind it a little.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can try but we don't have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this part was not transcribed. We have 15 page transcription. But the transcription does not cover this part.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, that's correct, Your Honour. If the interpreters can do their best. If we can just go back a frame, a few frames.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] You could see, this is one part, you could see what's there, well, you've seen where they are and under what circumstances, it is what it is. [In English] We will have no other choice but to say in our report that they did not fulfil Dr. Karadzic's promises and allow us [overlapping speakers on the videotape] [Interpretation] Well, tell Karadzic it's not allowed for you to see it for security reasons except for one part. You see, the war is being waged nearby. Well, then we won't be able to say that this is not a concentration camp. "The man in uniform: Have you seen women, have you seen children? No, you haven't. All these men are those who participated in the fighting with a gun. They had 2.500 people under arms. Only Kozarac had 3.000."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to the second clip and that's at 3.22, please. And we stopped at 3 -- 2.37, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "Male Reporter: [Some English] Why are you not fulfilling Dr. Karadzic's promises to us? "Red Cross Rep: He promised something else and said you can do this and this and that and not that. If they say this is a protocol of your stay here --"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, is that getting interpreted?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But the woman is talking in English. You mean interpreted into B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, please. If we can just go back again to start it at 3.22, and if you can please interpret for Mr. Mejakic what Mrs. Balaban is saying after the gentleman reporter says about Mr. Karadzic's -- fulfilling Dr. Karadzic's wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Mejakic, I want you to listen very carefully to what she says in relation to his question about Mr. Karadzic. So that's who he's talking about when he she responds.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can play it now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "Male Reporter: Okay. So why, why... "Penny Marshal: What's your reason? "Red Cross Rep: Just trying to do my best here. "[Overlapping speakers on videotape] "Red Cross Rep: Oh well... "Male Reporter: Why are you not fulfilling Dr. Karadzic's promise to us? "Red Cross Rep: He promised us something else and said you can do this and this and that and not that. If they say this is a protocol of your stay here..."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mejakic, he says why can't we do what Mr. Karadzic said, and Mrs. Balaban says, he told us something else. He said you can see this and this but not that. Now, that's the reality of it, isn't it, that it was agreed that these journalists wouldn't get in to see all of the detainees who were in all the other parts of the camp and the only thing that they were allowed to see was a couple of dozen men running over to get some food in the canteen. Because it was agreed that they wouldn't be allowed to see all of the detainees. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: That's not the impression that I gained, that it had been agreed before, because you saw earlier on in the footage, a moment before, when Simo Drljaca is saying something like what I said in my statement, that they were complaining to Karadzic -- or rather that they should complain to Karadzic, and then there is a part of the footage where he says -- or Milutinovic says, We are going to Trnopolje. This here is over. That's the bit that the cameras filmed. But there were things said outside of the range of the camera. Because Simo Drljaca did not allow them to visit the rest of the compound, specifically the area called the hangar, where these detainees coming in for lunch were running from.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was on the first clip. We saw that and we heard what -- what Simo Drljaca was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was not reflected in the transcript, was it, when Drljaca said tell Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's there, 64, line 1. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, so that was what we saw in that first clip and then the second clip was when the specific question was why can't we see what Mr. Karadzic says, that he had told them that they could see, and she specifically says, he told us something else. He said you can see this, and this, but not that. Words to that effect. We heard it.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I would not like to comment. I'm really not qualified to comment or to speculate whether this visit had been arranged and agreed in advance or not. You see what my role was, what I knew was that Karadzic had allowed them to visit but the circumstances of the visit were dictated by Simo Drljaca, and if I'm not mistaken this male journalist, I don't know his name, was particularly angry, and this young lady is called Penny Marshal, I believe, this male journalist was especially angry that they were not allowed to visit the hangar. I'm not sure whether the camera has recorded it but he was very, very angry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has seen that footage, Mr. Mejakic. You testified that you had received lists on 5 August as to who was going to be transferred to Manjaca and Trnopolje, and -- and that the next day, on 6 August, was when they were all transferred either to Manjaca or Trnopolje. It's right, isn't it, that once the vast majority of detainees were moved off to Manjaca and Trnopolje, that a few hundred military bunk beds or army cots were shipped in, weren't they? This occurred between the night of the 6th and 7th of August. You said that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I said but I didn't say several hundred. I said 170 to 180 approximately. Not several hundred.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. There was 175 to 180 detainees that were kept back that weren't sent to Manjaca or Trnopolje, but I'm saying that there were a few hundred military beds that were delivered to the Omarska camp the night in between the night of the 6th and the 7th of August; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But again, it's not a few hundred, it's up to 200 at most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then from that point on, the remaining detainees got two meals a day, you say that were better more nutritious, and from that day, as far as you were aware, nobody was maltreated in any way whatsoever. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that part of my testimony and I can affirm that what I said was true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so who -- who worked at the camp then between 7 and 21 August?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: The security service from the ranks of the police, inspectors, their coordinators, and all the other services, but their volumes were reduced.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And besides the foreign media visiting again on 7 August with Ostojic, you said in your statement that you also had a visit from ICRC and there was also a republic-level-appointed commission visit, wasn't there, to your very pristine camp with its -- with the new military beds?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, on 12 August, a delegation of the International Committee of the Red Cross paid us a visit, and the commission was not from the republican level. It was a commission that was established pursuant to a decision by the chief of the regional centre of the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, but it was not an official visit from anybody at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we pause there, we will get on to that after lunch.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will -- yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we rise for lunch I neglected to introduce our legal intern Romina Arnaudova who is from Bulgaria and today is her last day with our team. She has been with us quite a while. We appreciate her work very, very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We resume at 1.23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We left off before lunch discussing the visit by the -- you said there was a commission set up by CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could call up D01814, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned before we broke that Zupljanin set up this commission. And we can see here that -- in the first paragraph who he appointed. Number 1, Vojin Bera. He was the deputy chief of the centre for state security in the CSB Banja Luka, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: You are right. He was chief of the state security department, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he was Mirko Jesic's immediate supervisor, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's the Mirko Jesic, the SMB operative who worked at the camp. We are talking about the same person?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see Bera who he visited the Omarska camp? I'm talking about earlier when it was established. I'm not talking about in August. I'm talking about when he came to the camp before. Did you ever see him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The second one is Vaso Skondric. He's from Banja Luka too, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he is from. I believe that at the time he was a police inspector, he was an inspector in the police. I believe that he is a native of Banja Luka but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. The third member is Ranko Mijic. Now this is the same Ranko Mijic who actually worked in the camp as one of the operative coordinators like Mirko Jesic, wasn't he? He was he was working for the public security interrogators, in charge of coordinating them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the fourth person is a person called Jugoslav Rodic. Now, is this the same Jugoslav Rodic from Sanski Most who worked in the Omarska and Keraterm camps as one of the state security interrogators?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. There were two Rodic's and I really can't tell them apart. There is Radomir Rodic and also Jugoslav Rodic and I was never able to tell the two of them apart. I never knew which one of them was Rado and which was one was Jugoslav. I know they both worked for the State Security Service but I don't know which one was which.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter number 18410, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before that document leaves the screen, we see that they have to comply by the 17th of August with their report into the detention facilities in three municipalities: Prijedor, Sanski Most and Bosanski Novi -- Bosanski Novi. I'm sorry, that document that we saw a moment ago on the screen was dated the 14th of August 1992, the one that set up the commission. So what we are looking at now is a document dated 20 January 1993, and it's a report on the activities of Prijedor SMB for the period between 1st of January and 31st of December 1992. If we could go to page 2, please, it lists there in the second paragraph -- I'm sorry, the Sanski Most SMB war section had 12 employees at the beginning of the year, and then if we go about eight lines down it says: Jugoslav Rodic. Do you see there, the following employees remained at the end of 1992, Jugoslav Rodic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I can't see that on the screen because I have only the first page on the screen still.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, if we can go to page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, it's gone too far. But in any event you can see here on this page, page 3, it talks about these people being operatives in the Omarska and Keraterm camps. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I can see here, and I don't know what page this is, where it says: On the 25th of May 1992, in cooperation with the workers of the SJB Prijedor, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page 3 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we can see there it's the same as what you're reading, on the 15th of May 1992, reserve members of the Prijedor and Sanski Most war sections were mobilised and they worked in investigation centres such as Omarska, Keraterm, and Krings. So we've established that the Jugoslav Rodic that we are talking about is actually the same one from Sanski Most who actually worked in the Omarska camp that's been appointed to this commission. You agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. I'm just saying that there are two men by the name of Rodic and I could never tell the two of them apart. I actually never bothered to try and tell the two of them apart.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mejakic, we can see here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6536, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So we can see here, Mr. Mejakic, that two of the four -- at least two of the four members of this commission are actually investigating what -- their actual function or what they were doing for the last three months. Isn't it? That's correct, isn't it? It's a bit like putting the fox in charge of the hen house, isn't it? You're asking Mr. Mijic and Mr. Rodic to investigate what they've actually been involved in doing.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: This is correct. This is correct. They were appointed as members of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so you said a moment -- you said before --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said this is correct, this is correct, that they were appointed as members of that commission. [In English] That's different than what is in transcript as if -- as if he agreed with the qualification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, do you agree with my qualification that -- that you -- what Mr. Zupljanin is doing is actually putting people -- appointing them to actually investigate themselves? You -- you agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I really would refrain from making such judgements. He had his own reasons and I really don't want to go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before lunch you said that the -- that this commission visited Omarska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that they visited Omarska. I didn't say that they visited Omarska. As far as I know, they did it in Prijedor. They did it in Prijedor. They -- some of them didn't need to visit Omarska because they were already there. And as for that report, as far as I know, and the report appeared in my case as well, they actually drafted the report in Prijedor. Mr. Skondric and Ms. Kobero [phon], while I was in Omarska I never saw the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, I mentioned before lunch a republic-level visit. Mr. Lalai [phon] and Mr. Irkic [phon], do you remember them visiting the Omarska camp? Between the 10th and 15th of August?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that visit. I heard that the visit had taken place. It is possible that I wasn't there on that day, but I really can't remember that I met them in Omarska, ever. I suppose that they may have been in Prijedor, but I didn't see them. I know that they did come and I know what the occasion was but I didn't see them myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for Your Honour's reference, the CSB commission report is Exhibit D470.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, so then you wouldn't have read their report, Mr. Lalai and Mr. Irkic's report, and that's Exhibit P3549, dated the 17th of August 1992. In that report, they talk about a self-service canteen and beds and nurses. This is completely inapposite to the conditions in the camp a week before, isn't it, when you had 3.000 people in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. This is opposite to the situation that existed before. There were fewer prisoners, the conditions were much improved, and when you mentioned the figure of 3.000 detainees, I have to share a truth with you: There was never a time when Omarska held 3.000 people at any one time. According to the official data that was accepted by the court here and in Sarajevo, a total number of people who were detained in Omarska is 3400 but not 3.000 of them at any one time. People came and went and came and went.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. So on the 6th of August you transfer something like 1.331 to Manjaca. So that's 1300. And then you've got -- you've got 175 that stay behind, so that's over 1500. And of course there is other evidence that there is a figure of 1500 being transferred to Manjaca. But leaving that aside, the figure of I think 1.773 go to Trnopolje. Now, how many -- how many of those people went to Trnopolje? The women went early, they went on the 3rd of August, and then the men went later on the 6th of August, and there is evidence that there was buses going backwards and forwards and backwards and forwards between Omarska and Trnopolje. So on your estimate, how many people were transferred out of Omarska to Trnopolje on the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Certainly not as many as you say. Your figure is 1700 but it was much less. The transfer to Trnopolje started earlier. Transfers to Trnopolje started in early June, and I believe that the figure that is mentioned with regard to Trnopolje is the total number of those who were gradually transferred from the very beginning. It is true that most of them were transferred on 6 August. That is a fact. I really can't give you any numbers, but the number would be much lower than the 1700 that is referred as the official figure. They did go to Trnopolje, sometimes 50 on one occasion, 120 on the other, 160. On the 3rd of August, around 140 or 150 were transferred. So, yes, they may all have been transferred to Trnopolje but not as all of them or as many of them in just one go.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. And then you escorted the last group of inmates from the Omarska camp to Manjaca on the 21st of August or thereabouts, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: [Non-verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to just now come back to something that you spoke of earlier when you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to hear his answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. He did -- he said yes, Your Honour. It's not in the transcript. I'm sorry, Mr. Mejakic, your "yes" wasn't picked up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please bear in mind there is a gap between your answer and the moment he hears you -- he hears you out. Okay, did you answer yes, Mr. Mejakic? Did you escort the last group on 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say anything. I just nodded. I just nodded by way of saying yes, it is correct, on the 21st of August the last group was transferred to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So earlier today, you -- it's your position that crimes were infrequently committed by the security service, the security guards from the police, the active and reserve police force that were working in the Omarska camp. What your trial chamber found in -- in Bosnia in relation to Momcilo Gruban who was one of the shift leaders -- shift commanders, they found that there were killings of detainees directly and personally committed by persons during Gruban's shift and over whom he had effective control, and that there were beatings and physical assaults on the detainees directly and personally committed by persons during his shift and over whom he had control. And in relation to Milica Kos who was one of the other shift commanders, the Kvocka trial chamber here at this Tribunal found that [As read] "evidence establishes beyond reasonable doubt that Kos was directly and personally involved in beatings of detainees around mid-July 1992," and it also found that [As read] "Kos was involved in the extortion of detainees and stealing money from detainees in Omarska camp. And in that context, it can be characterised as part of the harassment inflicted upon the detainees in the camp. They also said that he was aware of the abusive treatment and conditions prevailing in the camp. And in relation to the third shift leader, Mladjo Radic, the same trial chamber, they were tried together, found that [As read] "Radic in his role as a guard shift leader was exposed on a daily basis to killings, tortures, and other abuses committed in the camp against the non-Serb detainees" and that [As read] "He knew that crimes of extreme physical and mental violence were being routinely committed in the camp for discriminatory purposes." And they also found or they also received [As read] "a substantial amount of credible and consistent evidence that a large number of crimes were committed by guards on Radic's shift and that [As read] "These guards perpetrated abuses of and mistreatment against the detainees including murder and torture." Now, Radic was also charged with rapes, as you know. Did you ever do anything in relation to these three shift commanders in relation to the crimes that they and their guards were committing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in my evidence before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I spoke about that, and by chance I had several pieces of physical evidence on the crimes that were committed on both sides, and I knew who they were committed by.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Pause there. You said in your trial in Bosnia that you wrote a number of official notes to Simo Drljaca, but did you ever try and do anything about having these people removed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: In view of my position, I was not able to undertake measures such as removal from work, suspension, or some other things. It was in the hands of the chief of the public security station and higher levels. What I could do was to draft an official note to forward it to the chief, and he was the one who decided what to do with the individuals in question. There were some examples where we intervened personally on our own in order to prevent abuses by those whom I wouldn't call policemen but irresponsible people who got to wear police uniforms by accident. A person, a reserve police officer, was arrested when he tried to extort money from a detainee. In general terms, what I can say is that things did happen. However, those were all acts committed by irresponsible individuals, by the people who were opportunists, when there was a war going on, there was a state of lawlessness, and they benefitted from that in order to come to their personal material gain or to settle scores, previous scores with some of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move on now, Mr. Mejakic. You -- you participated in a cover-up, didn't you? You lied publicly when giving interviews to the media, and you lied when you testified about many incidents and the fate of these individuals.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you were -- you gave an interview to Monika Gras in 1993, and in that interview you said that, as well as going on about the detainees getting two cooked meals a day and beds to lay on and a doctor and a medicine chest, which we know full well that may have been the case after the 6th of August, but it wasn't for the majority of the duration of the camp's existence. But you also said to her that no one was killed, only two died of natural causes, didn't you? You said that? And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think it would be good if she would just give the witness a chance hear the interpretation and give his answer before launching into the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, did you say that to Monika Gras?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: This is partly true. I had an opportunity in my own case to look at one excerpt from that interview, and it is true that I said about two individuals that they died of natural causes. Since I was not in charge of providing such information, I referred Monika Gras to my superiors at the public security station in Prijedor, but you can't see that in the transcript or in the recording. Second of all, when I spoke about health services that we provided, I didn't lie at all. From the very beginning until mid-July, we had a military doctor present, Slobodan Gajic was his name, I believe, and there was also an ambulance on the grounds. Services were provided to the extent possible. The situation was what it was. There were no medicines, there was no electricity. There was no food. And when I spoke to Monika Gras and when I told her about beds I told her the truth. From 6th of --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: August.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: From the 6th of August onwards, beds were installed and in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But she was -- she was basically asking you what the camp was like and you -- you came up with this. But just getting back to the doctor that you said that was in the camp, there was evidence in your trial that he didn't -- that he left the camp and it was -- and it was actually Dr. Eso Sadikovic, the Muslim doctor who was detained in the camp, that was actually one that was helping the detainees most in relation to any medical needs they had, wasn't it? Not Dr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: May I answer? Dr. Gajic left in mid-July. After that, Dr. Ivic was the doctor who went to Omarska every day. The health practitioners arrived from the outpatient's clinic in Omarska. It is true that there was a detainee, Esad Sadikovic, who administered aid to the detainees, and he's not the only one. There were other doctors who did the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: We managed to obtain some medicines which we placed at the disposal of Dr. Sadikovic and the other one whose name was possibly Dr. Begic, but I'm not sure, and there was another younger doctor who was there whose name I cannot recall at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Jusuf Pasic from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Dr. Begic died, didn't he? He was killed in Omarska or he was taken away?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Begic was taken from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, you were cross-examined about this Monika Gras interview at your trial, and you said that you didn't tell the truth because this was the official version and that nobody dared change anything to that when talking to the media. And when prosecutor Peter Kidd asked you whether you were concerned that if the truth came out you might be held accountable for your role in the Omarska camp and that's why you were continuing to say the line that you were saying, you responded that you weren't concerned in that regard at all. You said: [As read] "Why would I be concerned about some things that were done in that way, some things are being kept secrets from public. Nothing can be concealed. There is nothing that can be concealed in this world." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember having said it in that way. I only said that after such a long time, there were no secrets any more. I don't think that there are any secrets about the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Prijedor. You know people who were killed on the firing line by name, although it will still take a lot of time to untangle all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You happily went along with it and participated in this cover-up so that the truth didn't come out and so that you and others involved in these barbaric events were never prosecuted. That's what you were hoping.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No. I never hoped that I would be able to avoid court process. I surrendered voluntarily to this Tribunal, having been aware of that and on one occasion --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We will get to that but I just have one other area that I want to deal with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, may he be allowed to complete his answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it wasn't in -- it wasn't responsive to my question. He was going into another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Maybe he was getting to the responsive part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he not answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He said I had never hoped that I would be able to avoid court process. And then he wanted to go on and talk about his surrender. I'm not interested just for the moment in his surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: The question involved, did it not, whether he participated in this cover-up. He didn't get a chance to answer that, did he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mejakic, please continue, if you would like to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was never my intention to participate in the cover-up of anything that would be illegal or could be incriminated. Never. I was not duty-bound to do so but I testified before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina for five days. At the end of the day, it suffices to look at the final court decision which took into account my evidence to understand how sincere and honest I was in what I said before the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, you kept a number of documents in -- related to the Omarska camp and the events there in your locker at the Omarska Police Station, didn't you, and you testified about that in your trial?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, just going back to when I said to you that the Prosecutor had questioned you about whether were you concerned if the truth came out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have that on the screen, please, if -- that's 25703E, and if we could go to page 47.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So just there, Mr. Prosecutor says were you concerned, Mr. Mejakic, if the truth came out you might be held accountable for your role at the Omarska camp, and you said no, no I was not concerned in that regard at that time, nor I thought of it. Why would I be concerned about some things that were done in that way, some things that have been kept secrets from public. Nothing can be concealed. There is no thing that can be concealed in this world. So you said that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is part of my answer and I don't see anything disputable. Nothing from my answer indicates the fact that I was trying to conceal anything. This is how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I understood you to say you answered it a little bit differently. But anyway, we will get back to what we were dealing with about the documents that you kept in your locker. You said in 1996 at the time IFOR troops and the international police started arriving in the area, that upon an order of the head of the centre for public security, Simo Drljaca, who was back in his old post by that stage, that he ordered that all documentation pertaining to the wartime period in 1992 was collected and burnt including the documents you referred to earlier that you'd kept in the police branch office in Omarska. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were indicted by ICTY in February 1995 for your participation in crimes in the Omarska camp in 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: One moment. And you testified in cross-examination that in November 1996, you were told by Kijac, who was the then Minister of the Interior, Dragan Kijac, through Mijic, that's Ranko Mijic, the then-Prijedor SJB head, to step down from your position in the Omarska Police Station, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were provided a false ID by the RS MUP and you went to Serbia, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I did go to Serbia, but without any false documentation issued by Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 25703 -- sorry, 25703C, please. If we can go to page 32. Is that exhibit coming up?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mejakic, we can see here that your defence counsel said you ceased working in the police, when and why, and then you said in November 1996, and then you go on to talk about Kijac. He sent you a message that you should step down. What happened, what did you do. Well for a while I was at home. In the meantime, all my personal document was taken away, my ID card, my driver's licence, and I was told I should step aside. And then if we can go to the next page: I simply sat on a bus with a falsified ID card. It was not a falsified ID card with respect to the authenticity and the stamp. I was issued by the Ministry of the Interior card to a false name, and I went to Serbia and I stayed there until surrendering to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: This is not clear to me. It was not 1996. I left in 1998. I never said that I went with a false ID to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, this is what it says here, you sat on a bus with a falsified ID, not in relation to the stamp but an ID card with a false name that was given to you by the Ministry of Interior. That's what it says on those top four lines. You can see in front of you. I've just read it -- the text to you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: This simply does not correspond to what I said to the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if I can remember correctly. First of all, I did not leave by bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that page and the previous page. Starting in November 1996, the then Minister of Interior Kijac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: That's why I would like to see the original. No matter it is uploaded or not. And even if there is an audio. If there is an audio, because witness did not agree with this assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive this, two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P6537, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mejakic, I'm sorry, I called up the wrong page a moment ago when I was dealing with Monika Gras, and so I would like to go back to the answer that you gave when were you interviewed by her.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's at 65 ter number 25703E.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When I asked you a moment ago when you were cross-examined at your trial and you said that you didn't tell the truth because there was this -- the official version, you didn't -- you didn't answer my question in relation to that. You did say that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: Regarding all my addresses to members of the media, and after September 1992, there was a report provided by the commission that you mentioned a while ago and presented evidence about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But, Mr. Mejakic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, my question was did you say what I -- what I read to you, that you didn't tell the truth because this was the official version? Is that what you said? Do you remember saying that in -- when you -- when you were cross-examined in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can have page 46, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't remember saying that in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So the Prosecutor said, why did you not tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we start from the previous page?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, this is -- this is the Prosecutor putting to you the -- what you said on the tape about the prisoners, there were no killings here. Two men have died here of natural death. You may check it up at Prijedor. And then he asks you did you give that answer, Mr. Mejakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then if we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and was --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Please, could it be read verbatim and translated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's go back to the previous page. Please read out the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor says: [As read] "Did you go on to say this, Mr. Mejakic, I'll give you the question first, and then I'll give you the answer: 'The prisoners,' this is the question, 'The prisoners with whom I talked have told me of torture and murder. What do you have to say to that?' "And did you give this answer: "'No. I mean, this is not the first time I am asked this question, myself and my boss. There were no killings here. Two men have died here of a natural death. You may check it up at Prijedor.' "Did you give that answer, Mr. Mejakic? "You replied: "Yes, yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: "Q. And was that the truth?" Your response: "No, it wasn't."

utterances.speaker: MR. PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: "Why did you not tell the truth?" Your answer: "In the part ... the response to your question, in the part of my response, when I mention that my boss was asked that question, this was the official version that Simo Drljaca informed the journalist about all the time, one could see it in the newspapers and on TV. And finally, there was an official report of the commission ... of a commission which investigated these issues, and this was an official information and nobody dared to change anything to that when talking to media, let alone myself to be ... to dare change anything. You are right, it was not truth what I've stated and now I explained you why this was the case." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I did say that. A moment ago I didn't understand you properly. I'm sorry, but your questions are long, long, long. So I find myself in a situation not knowing exactly what you're asking me about. This is true. This is what I said. And I think that it happened during cross-examination by Prosecutor Peter kid. And that is the truth, that it happened this way, because I had an order just like everybody else who communicated with the journalists were ordered to provide an official version, which actually meant that they were relating and paraphrasing the commission report. It did not apply to me only. Drljaca gave a lot of statements to the media as did many other officials from the public security station et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this commission report is the CSB Banja Luka commission report, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. Mejakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency. I'll start with the most recent one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mejakic, did you give a statement to this journalist under oath?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 76 of today's transcript, there was mention of Gruban's shift, this was happening on this shift, the other things were happening on that shift. Were there any differences in the way detainees were treated by different shifts?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: The differences were evident. The trial conducted in Sarajevo has proven beyond a reasonable doubt, and it is contained in the judgement, according to witness statement was that this shift was an exemplary one and that when they were on duty, all the prisoners felt most relaxed. I am just quoting their words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which shift are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Gruban's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that there were shifts that were not exemplary and what did it depend on?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: The selection of people for the reserve police force, and a very small number of professional policemen, was the root of the problem. We were able to influence the selection of people to be admitted into reserve force up until one point, that is to say when the conflict broke out, but in the aftermath of the conflict, the situation became chaotic. The system was in the process of inception, and it so happened that people with criminal past happened to find themselves in the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, both Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mejakic put a pause between the question and answers. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the conduct during certain shifts as a kind of desirable one in view of the chief of the station and in your view as the chief of security?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: If all in the security service, starting from the police to members of the TO, were like the people from Gruban's shift, I believe that nobody from the police ranks would end up in a court of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 51, you were shown Prosecution Exhibit P4855, which indicates that people who were taken away in one group were later found in three different graves. Was there any investigation conducted on that matter to find out how they met their death, whether somebody were exchanged, and whether they resumed the fighting?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: My knowledge is limited concerning this matter. I know that there were cases when people were supposed to be exchanged. However, the exchange never took place. Instead, they were being shifted from one location to another. All kinds of things were happening, maybe that is one of the explanations. As for the fact that people from one group were later found in three different locations, and I'm talking about their remains, believe me I have no clue as how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 50, it was said that some people were taken away and were never seen again. Can you tell us what was a possible outcome if a person is taken away and never returned?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please pause between questions and answers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? Please wait for some time after Mr. Karadzic's answer. Yes, if you could repeat your answer, Mr. Mejakic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'll try to abide by your warning. There was a possibility for a person or a group to be transferred to a remand prison in Tunica, the military remand prison in Stari Gradiska or to Trnopolje or to Manjaca. So these were the options that were available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any instances when there were private exchanges or individual exchanges?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I have no specific knowledge about that. I have some indirect indications and knowledge that certain individuals were involved in private exchanges, such as my former colleagues from the Yugoslav People's Army who happened to find themselves in the opposite side, and they reached some kind of mutual agreements and arrangements to do that. But this is second-hand knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that it happened sometimes that people who were once taken prisoner then exchanged and then taken prisoner again?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That happened very often, specifically with regard to certain individuals from the Kozarac area. I clearly remember that some people were taken prisoners twice as members of the army of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Investigator Ago Sadikovic was mentioned. Can you tell the Chamber what his ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak or a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 30 onwards, you were asked about the Prosecutions of perpetrators of certain crimes and you, yourself, said that eventually they were prosecuted. Can you tell us whether the documentation collected at the time was used in those trials against them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On a couple occasions, as far as I know, and probably in other cases as well, the documentation compiled in 1992 was used both by this Tribunal and national courts as well. People tend to forget that some people were even tried during the war for crimes committed against not only against Serbs but also against Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Some of your associates, Jesic or whoever, told you that somebody would be liable for that sooner or later. How did you construe that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult how I understood that at that particular moment. I realised that this person was talking about something that he had no detailed knowledge of. I was more prone to understand this as his attempt to evade his responsibility, possible responsibility, for the commission of deeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It has been suggested or, rather, it was read to you from the judgement handed down by the Bosnian court that people were detained arbitrarily, that is on page 18, line 12. You agreed that this is what is written in the judgement, but did you agree with the assertion that people were brought in arbitrarily and without any grounds whatsoever, the majority of the people?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I said that what is written in the judgement is something that I cannot alter. The truth is the following: I don't believe that more than five to ten people -- per cent of people were arrested arbitrarily in this first wave of arrests. All the arrests that followed later on were the result of intelligence work of inspectors, and there is a large number of cases containing the list of people that need to be brought to the remand prison in Omarska, there is a list of people who made these recommendations, and there is the signature of the person who approved that, and then it also states who conducted the arrests and who brought the individuals to Omarska. So the arrests took place on the basis of intelligence inquiries in most cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. P05519 was shown to you. It's a list of 76 people in the first category. In keeping with your previous answer, can you tell us how operative work resulted in a list of people who needed to be brought in and investigated?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I did not participate in the investigations, but from what I know, from talking to one of the detainees, you come to the name of another one and then another one. By talking to people you get other names.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I show the witness 1D9523? It's possible there is no translation for it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what kind of document this is and who made it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: This is an Official Note done in the unit for crime prevention and detection in Banja Luka, dated 25th March 1993, and it relates to an interview done with Hamdija Beslagic from Kozarosani [phon] Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, what is it said he had done with his wife and daughter before the outbreak of the war? This sentence that begins with "in February, I..."?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MEJAKIC
utterances.text: I'll read it out. "In February 1992, I sent my wife Jasminka and daughter Marina born 1970 --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just wondering how this arises from cross-examination, going into a -- the operative note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
